opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the more interesting questions right now. For most of the past decade the story was fairly simple: you take a larger model, train it on more data, use more compute, and you get predictable improvements in loss and, roughly, in downstream capabilities. The data side of that equation was mostly about quantity, just scraping more of the internet.

What's changed is that the high-quality, human-generated text on the public web is finite. When we looked at this at Epoch, the stock of useful public text is large but not unbounded, and at current rates of scaling, frontier labs start to bump up against it within years rather than decades. So the question becomes: what fills the gap?

Reasoning data is a big part of the answer. Most web text isn't particularly dense in the kind of signal you want if you're trying to get a model to do multi-step problem solving: careful math, debugging code, working through a scientific argument. A worked solution to a hard problem, where you see intermediate steps and can verify the final answer, is plausibly worth far more per token than a random forum post. So the effective value of the data matters, not just the token count.

The exciting part is that reasoning data is something you can increasingly generate with compute. In domains where answers are verifiable, like math, programming, and some formal sciences, you can have the model attempt many solutions, check which ones are correct, and train on those. That turns the data constraint partly back into a compute problem, which is the kind of problem the field has been very good at scaling through. Reinforcement learning on verifiable tasks is basically this loop.

So I'd say the relationship is complementary. Scale gives you a model capable enough to produce useful reasoning traces, and those traces make the next round of scaling more efficient. There are open questions. How well does this transfer to domains where you can't easily verify the answer? Do you get diminishing returns or something like model collapse if you lean too heavily on self-generated data? I don't think we know yet. But my general view is that the data wall is less of a hard wall than people sometimes suggest, precisely because reasoning data can be manufactured with compute, and that's a key reason I expect scaling to keep delivering meaningful gains for a while.

r001.rationale: The candidate says scaling produces a model capable enough to generate useful reasoning traces.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the relationship has shifted quite a bit over the past couple of years, and I've updated on it.

For a long time, the scaling story was pretty simple: more parameters, more compute, more data, and you got predictable improvements in loss and downstream performance. The data side of that was mostly about quantity. You scraped more of the web, you filtered a bit, and you were largely relying on the model to extract whatever reasoning signal was latent in that text.

What's changed is that the bottleneck has partly moved. We're approaching the limits of high-quality human-generated text on the web, and at the same time we've found that targeted reasoning data, whether that's carefully curated chain-of-thought, verified solutions to math and code problems, or synthetic data generated and filtered by other models, gives you a disproportionate return per token. So the marginal value of a token is now very uneven. A token of verified multi-step reasoning is worth far more than a token of generic web prose.

That said, I'd push back against the framing that this is a replacement for scaling. I think of it more as a complement that changes the exchange rate. You still need a large base model to absorb and generalize from that reasoning data. A small model trained on beautiful reasoning traces hits a ceiling fairly quickly. What the high-quality data does is let you convert compute into capability more efficiently, and in particular it lets you shift compute from pretraining into post-training and inference-time reasoning, where you're generating, verifying, and reinforcing the model's own problem-solving.

So in terms of the trajectory, I don't think the data constraint stops progress. What it does is make the question of where the data comes from much more important. Increasingly the answer is that models are generating their own training signal in domains where you can verify correctness, like math and code. The open question for me is how far that extends into domains where verification is harder, because that's where the real economic value lives, and that's where I'd put a lot of my uncertainty about the next few years.

r001.rationale: The response says larger base models can absorb and generalize from reasoning data, and that models can generate training signals. It does not state that increasing model size enables higher-quality reasoning traces.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re complementary. Scaling up a model gives it more capacity to learn, but what it learns depends on the data you give it. If you want it to reason well, there’s potentially a lot of value in examples that show how to work through a difficult problem, rather than just stating the answer.

The challenge is that high-quality reasoning data is relatively scarce. So one promising approach is to use models to generate candidate solutions and then check which ones are correct. That’s particularly useful in domains like mathematics and programming, where you can often verify an answer more easily than you can produce it.

That creates a potential feedback loop: better models can help produce better training data, which can then improve subsequent models. But you have to distinguish between reasoning that actually leads to reliable answers and text that merely looks like good reasoning. So I wouldn’t view better data as replacing scale. It can make scaling more effective, while scale can help us generate and use better data.

r001.rationale: The response says scaling can help generate better data, and in context that data includes reasoning examples; it also says better models can produce better training data.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re complementary. Scaling gives you more capacity to learn, but the quality of the data determines what you learn to do with that capacity. For reasoning, that means examples that contain useful intermediate steps, explore different approaches, and arrive at answers you can actually verify.

There’s also a feedback loop: more capable models can generate candidate solutions, and where you can check those solutions—say, in mathematics or programming—you can select the successful ones and use them for further training. That potentially lets you produce reasoning data beyond what humans have written down.

The challenge is that a correct final answer doesn’t necessarily imply good reasoning, and verification is much harder in some domains than others. So I wouldn’t see high-quality reasoning data as replacing scaling. It’s one of the things that can make additional scale more productive.

r001.rationale: The response says more capable models can generate candidate solutions that can be checked and selected for training, but it does not clearly state that increasing model size enables generation of higher-quality reasoning traces.
